1.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **silence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [may you not be silent]

The expressions **do not be still** and **do not be quiet** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [do not remain inactive]

The psalmist is using the imperative forms **do not be still** and **do not be quiet** to make a request to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a natural form for making a request. Alternate translation: [please do not be still, and please do not be quiet]

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [do not remain silent and inactive]

2.note: The psalmist uses **For behold** to introduce the reason for his plea in verse 1. He is saying that God should take action because the enemies are rising up. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make the connection clearer.

The word **behold** is used here to draw attention to what follows. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this with a word or phrase that serves this purpose, or you could leave it untranslated. Alternate translation: [look]

The phrase **the ones hating you** refers to the same people as **your enemies** earlier in the verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [those same enemies of yours]
See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [your enemies are boldly rising up against you]

The expression **lift up the head** is an idiom that means to act boldly or defiantly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [act defiantly]

3.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [they are craftily plotting against your cherished people]
The pronoun **They** refers to the enemies mentioned in verse 2. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [Your enemies are cunning]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **counsel**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in counseling together]

The phrase **your treasured ones** refers to the people of Israel, whom God values. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [the Israelites, your treasured people]

4.note: The pronoun **They** refers to the enemies mentioned in verses 2–3. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [These enemies have said]

Here, **the name of Israel** represents the nation of Israel itself and its existence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the nation of Israel]

If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that no one may remember the name of Israel]

5.note: The word **For** introduces the reason why the psalmist said what he said in verses 3–4. The enemies are conspiring because they want to destroy Israel. Use a connector in your language that introduces a reason. Alternate translation: [This is because]
The pronoun **they** refers to the nations listed in verses 6–8. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [these nations have conspired]

Here, **heart** represents the will or intention. The psalmist is saying that these enemies have **conspired** with unified purpose. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with one purpose]

The expression **they have cut a covenant** is an idiom that means they have made a formal agreement or alliance. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have allied themselves]

6.note: The psalmist is leaving out the verb that would be expected in this phrase. The verb can be supplied from the context in verse 5. If it would be helpful in your language, you could supply this verb. Alternate translation: [the tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites have cut a covenant against you]

Here, **the tents of Edom** represents the people of Edom who live in those tents. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the people of Edom]

7.note: The psalmist is leaving out the verb that would be expected in this phrase. The verb can be supplied from the context in verse 5. If it would be helpful in your language, you could supply this verb. Alternate translation: [Gebal and Ammon and Amalek have cut a covenant against you]

8.note: The pronoun **they** refers to Assyria, mentioned earlier in the verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [the Assyrians]

8.q: גַּם־אַ֭שּׁוּר נִלְוָ֣ה עִמָּ֑⁠ם הָ֤י֥וּ זְר֖וֹעַ לִ⁠בְנֵי־ל֣וֹט
8.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [Also Assyria has joined with them; indeed, they {are} an arm to the sons of Lot]

Here, **an arm** represents military strength or support. The psalmist is saying that Assyria has provided military power to help the descendants of Lot. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have given military support to the sons of Lot]

The psalmist is speaking of **the sons of Lot** to mean the descendants of Lot, that is, the Moabites and Ammonites. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Lot]

9.note: The psalmist is using the imperative form **Do to them as to Midian** to make a request to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a natural form for making a request. Alternate translation: [Please do to them as to Midian]

10.note: The pronoun **They** refers to Midian, Sisera, and Jabin mentioned in verse 9. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [Those enemies were destroyed]
If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [God destroyed them]

The psalmist is speaking of the dead enemies as if **they became dung for the ground**. He means that their corpses were left unburied and decayed on the ground like refuse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [their dead bodies lay rotting on the ground]

11.note: The psalmist uses the word **like** to compare the fate he requests for the current enemies to the fate of **Oreb** and **Zeeb**, who were Midianite commanders killed by Gideon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [Defeat them and their nobles as Gideon defeated Oreb and Zeeb]

The psalmist is using the imperative form **Make them, their nobles** to make a request to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a natural form for making a request. Alternate translation: [Please make them, their nobles]

The psalmist is using the adjective **nobles** as a noun to refer to people who are noble. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate it with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [their noble leaders]

The psalmist uses the word **like** to compare the fate he requests for the princes of the current enemies to the fate of **Zebah** and **Zalmunna**, who were Midianite kings defeated by Gideon. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [and defeat all of their princes as Gideon defeated Zebah and Zalmunna]

The psalmist is using the adjective **princes** as a noun to refer to people who are princely rulers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate it with an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [their ruling princes]

12.note: The pronoun **who** refers to the nobles and princes mentioned in verse 11. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [Those nobles and princes]

The psalmist is speaking of the land of Israel as **the pastures of God**. He means the land that God has given to his people as their dwelling place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the land that God gave to his people]

The psalmist is using the possessive form **the pastures of God** to describe pastures that belong to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this relationship in another way. Alternate translation: [the pastures that belong to God]

13.note: The psalmist uses the word **like** to compare the enemies to **tumbleweed**, which is blown away by the wind. He means that God should scatter them completely. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [scatter them as the wind scatters tumbleweed]

The psalmist is using the imperative form **make them like tumbleweed** to make a request to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a natural form for making a request. Alternate translation: [please make them like tumbleweed]

The psalmist uses the word **like** to compare the enemies to **chaff** that is blown away by the wind. He means that God should scatter them as easily as the wind scatters chaff. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [like chaff blown away by the wind]

Here, **the face of the wind** represents the front of the wind, that is, the direction the wind blows. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before the wind]

14.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [As fire burns a forest; indeed, as a flame kindles mountains]

The psalmist uses the word **as** to compare his request for God’s action against the enemies to how **fire burns a forest** and how **flame kindles mountains**. He means that God should consume the enemies completely. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [As fire consumes a forest and as flames consume the mountainside]

15.note: The word **thus** connects the similes in verses 13–14 to the request in verse 15. The psalmist is saying that just as fire consumes a forest and flame kindles mountains, so God should pursue the enemies. Use a connector in your language that draws a comparison. Alternate translation: [in that way,]

The psalmist is using the imperative form **pursue them with your tempest** to make a request to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a natural form for making a request. Alternate translation: [please pursue them with your tempest]

See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [pursue and terrify them with your swirling tempest]

16.note: The psalmist is using the imperative form **Fill their faces with shame** to make a request to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a natural form for making a request. Alternate translation: [Please fill their faces with shame]

Here, **their faces** represents their public identity or reputation. The psalmist is asking God to bring shame upon these enemies publicly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Bring shame upon them publicly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Make them thoroughly ashamed]

The phrase **that they may seek your name** states the goal or purpose of the request in the first part of the verse. The psalmist is asking God to shame the enemies so that they will turn to God. Use a connector in your language that introduces a goal or purpose. Alternate translation: [to the end that they may seek your name]

Here, **your name** represents God himself and his authority. The psalmist is asking that the enemies would turn to seek God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that they may seek you]

17.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [May they be utterly shamed and destroyed forever]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **shame**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [May they be ashamed]

If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and may God terrify them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **disgrace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and may they be disgraced]

18.note: The phrase **may they know** refers to the enemies described in verses 2–8. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this explicit. Alternate translation: [And may those enemies know]
Asaph is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to his reputation. Alternate translation: [you are Yahweh]
